shortDescription: Learn Java from scratch — from basics to OOP, collections, and real-world projects.

modules.title: Introduction to Java
modules.description: What Java is, why it's used, and how to set it up.
modules.content:
Java is a high-level, object-oriented programming language developed by Sun Microsystems in 1995. It follows the principle of 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA), meaning compiled Java code can run on any platform that supports the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

Java is widely used in web development, Android apps, enterprise software, and backend systems.

To get started, install the JDK (Java Development Kit) from https://www.oracle.com/java and set up your PATH environment variable. You can use IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code.

modules.title: Variables and Data Types
modules.description: Understanding how Java stores and manages data.
modules.content:
Java is a statically typed language, meaning every variable must have a declared type.

Primitive types:
- int: whole numbers (e.g. 10, -5)
- double: decimal numbers (e.g. 3.14)
- char: single character (e.g. 'A')
- boolean: true or false
- long, float, short, byte: other numeric types

Reference types include String, arrays, and objects.

Variables must be declared before use. Java also supports type casting — converting one type to another.

modules.title: Operators and Expressions
modules.description: Arithmetic, relational, logical, and assignment operators in Java.
modules.content:
Java supports the following operator types:

1. Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % (modulus)
2. Relational: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=
3. Logical: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
4. Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=, /=
5. Increment/Decrement: ++, --
6. Ternary: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

Operator precedence follows standard math rules — use parentheses to control evaluation order.

modules.title: Control Flow — if, else, switch
modules.description: Making decisions in your Java programs.
modules.content:
Control flow statements let your program make decisions.

if-else: executes a block based on a condition.
else if: chains multiple conditions.
switch: matches a variable against multiple cases — cleaner than long if-else chains for fixed values.

Java 14+ also supports switch expressions with arrow syntax.

modules.title: Loops — for, while, do-while
modules.content:
Loops allow you to execute a block of code multiple times.

- for loop: best when you know the number of iterations.
- while loop: runs as long as a condition is true.
- do-while loop: runs at least once, then checks the condition.
- for-each loop: iterates over arrays or collections cleanly.

Use break to exit a loop early and continue to skip the current iteration.

modules.title: Methods (Functions)
modules.description: Writing reusable blocks of code with methods.
modules.content:
A method is a block of code that performs a specific task and can be called multiple times.

Method structure:
  returnType methodName(parameters) { body }

- void: method returns nothing.
- return: sends a value back to the caller.
- Parameters: inputs passed to the method.
- Overloading: multiple methods with the same name but different parameters.

Methods help keep code DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

modules.title: Arrays
modules.description: Storing and working with multiple values in a single variable.
modules.content:
An array stores a fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type.

- Declare: int[] arr = new int[5];
- Initialize: int[] arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
- Access: arr[0] (zero-indexed)
- Length: arr.length

2D arrays are arrays of arrays — useful for grids and matrices.

For dynamic sizing, use ArrayList from java.util instead.

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming — Classes & Objects
modules.description: The foundation of Java — modeling real-world entities with classes.
modules.content:
Java is an object-oriented language. Everything revolves around classes and objects.

- Class: a blueprint/template.
- Object: an instance of a class.
- Fields: variables that belong to a class.
- Constructor: a special method called when an object is created.
- this: refers to the current object.

OOP makes code modular, reusable, and easier to maintain.

modules.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
modules.description: Reusing and extending classes with inheritance.
modules.content:
Inheritance lets a class (child) inherit fields and methods from another class (parent) using the extends keyword.

- super: calls the parent class constructor or method.
- Method Overriding: child class redefines a parent method.
- Polymorphism: one interface, many implementations — a parent reference can hold a child object.

This reduces code duplication and enables flexible design.

modules.title: Interfaces and Abstraction
modules.description: Defining contracts and hiding implementation details.
modules.content:
An interface defines a contract — a set of methods a class must implement. It contains only method signatures (no body) by default.

Abstract classes are similar but can have both abstract and concrete methods.

Key differences:
- A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class.
- Use interfaces for defining capabilities (Runnable, Comparable).
- Use abstract classes for shared base behavior.

Interfaces are the backbone of Java's design patterns and frameworks.

modules.title: Exception Handling
modules.content:
Exceptions are runtime errors that can crash your program if unhandled. Java uses try-catch-finally blocks to handle them.

- try: code that might throw an exception.
- catch: handles the exception.
- finally: always runs (cleanup code).
- throw: manually throw an exception.
- throws: declares that a method may throw an exception.

Common exceptions: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException, IOException.

modules.title: Collections — ArrayList and HashMap
modules.description: Working with dynamic data structures in Java.
modules.content:
The Java Collections Framework provides ready-made data structures.

ArrayList: a resizable array.
- add(), remove(), get(), size(), contains()

HashMap: stores key-value pairs.
- put(), get(), remove(), containsKey(), keySet()

Other useful collections:
- LinkedList: doubly linked list
- HashSet: unique elements, no order
- TreeMap: sorted key-value pairs

Always use generics (e.g. ArrayList<String>) for type safety.
